title: Why 1746 happened
hook: a governor's minister, grieving his brother, turned on the Sikhs, and the loss that followed is remembered as the small holocaust

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sikh riders walked a departing army's captives home. Your line was captives brought home. Today, a darker turn.

A body is carried into Lahore. The dead man is Jaspat Rai, an official who rode out against a Sikh band and was killed in the fighting. His brother, Lakhpat Rai, is a minister at the governor's court. Tradition says Lakhpat Rai took off his turban, threw it down, and swore he would not put it on again until he had wiped the Sikhs out. One man's grief. Soon it had an army behind it. This path has already walked through what happened next, the small holocaust; today asks why.
screen: `A BROTHER KILLED.` → `A TURBAN THROWN DOWN.` → `A VOW OF REVENGE.`

segments.voice: The grief was real. Lakhpat Rai lost his brother. But watch what the grief turned into. Tradition says he didn't stop at the fighters: Sikhs living quietly in Lahore were rounded up. Tradition says he went further still: he ordered that the Sikh scriptures not be read, and even that the word gur, which means the Guru but is also the Punjabi word for brown sugar, not be spoken in the city. People were told to call the sugar something else. A man's sorrow had grown into a war on a whole people, down to a word in the market. The army marched, and the loss that followed is remembered as the Chhota Ghallughara. Now set beside that a word from the very first line of Sikh scripture, describing God: nirvair. Without hate, without enmity. And Guru Arjan in the Granth, in paraphrase: no one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger; I get along with everyone. That line sits in the same scripture the minister tried to silence. And look at how the story is kept. The Ardas, the prayer said at the end of gurdwara gatherings, remembers those who gave their lives for the faith. It remembers them; it doesn't curse anyone. The names of the dead are carried; the hatred isn't. Grief is not the danger. Grief is what love does when someone is taken. The danger is the moment grief decides someone must pay, and keeps widening the circle of who that someone is. Lakhpat Rai's story shows that moment; the Sikh way of remembering it shows grief without hate.
screen: `GRIEF THAT TURNED TO REVENGE.` · `EVEN A WORD WAS BANNED.` · `NIRVAIR: WITHOUT HATE.` · `REMEMBERED, NOT CURSED.` · then, large: `GRIEF WITHOUT HATE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a loss, yours or a wrong done to someone you love, one you can hold for two minutes, and let the sadness be there. If a wish that someone would pay rides along with it, set it gently apart, like a heavy bag beside you: keep the love, loosen the grip on the blame. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.
nirvair, without hate. Tradition says a minister's grief for his brother became a vow of revenge against a whole people, even though the opening line of Sikh scripture names God this way.
Your line: grief without hate. Sorrow can stay without the circle of blame growing. See you tomorrow.

notes: The index hook mentions 'thousands died'; per the claims rule no figure is given in the script. Year one (day 288) already gives estimates.
Jaspat Rai killed in a clash with a Sikh band (traditionally near Eminabad); Lakhpat Rai as diwan of the Lahore governor Yahiya Khan; the thrown-down turban and vow: confirm the telling.
The ban on reading Sikh scripture and on the word 'gur' (jaggery, to be called 'rori' instead) is a well-known tradition; confirm and decide whether to name 'rori'.
Paraphrase of Ang 1299 ('na ko bairi nahi bigana, sagal sang ham kau ban aai'): confirm Ang and attribution to Guru Arjan.
Lakhpat Rai's own religion is deliberately not mentioned so the story is not framed against any community; confirm this framing.
The line 'Grief is what love does when someone is taken' is the script's own image, not a Sikh teaching; confirm it reads that way.
